units.title: Unit 31 — Classroom language
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 31. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Classroom equipment, learning actions and functional requests
learningObjectives: Identify classroom equipment and explain what common items are used for.
Use look up, plug in, turn up/down, swap places and other study-related actions accurately.
Distinguish borrowing from lending and make polite classroom requests.
Ask about vocabulary meaning, pronunciation, spelling and usage.
Recognise key verb–noun relationships including pronounce/pronunciation and explain/explanation.

items.example: I found an old DVD of our school play.
items.note: A disc used to store video or other digital content; the book uses it as a classroom example.

items.example: The teacher switched on the DVD player.
items.note: Equipment for playing DVDs.

items.example: Can I use your rubber to erase this pencil mark?
items.note: British English for an eraser; it removes pencil writing.

items.example: Use a ruler to draw a straight line.
items.note: A straight tool for drawing lines and measuring length.

items.example: My pencil sharpener is in the front pocket of my bag.
items.note: A small tool for making a pencil point sharp.

items.example: She used a highlighter pen to mark important phrases.
items.note: A pen used to make words stand out in bright colour.

items.example: The plug was loose, so the screen went off.
items.note: The part of an electrical device inserted into a socket.

items.example: There is a socket behind the teacher's desk.
items.note: A point in a wall that supplies electricity to a plug.

items.example: Rub the pencil line out before you hand in your work.
items.note: British English; a separable phrasal verb. You can rub it out.

items.example: Please sharpen your pencil before the drawing activity.
items.note: Use a sharpener to make the pencil point sharp.

items.example: Measure the width of the page in centimetres.
items.note: Find the size, length or amount of something.

items.example: Highlight a word whenever you want to review it later.
items.note: Mark text to make it easy to notice.

items.example: I looked the new expression up in a dictionary.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: look it up, not look up it.

items.example: A learner's dictionary gives examples of common words.
items.note: A reference book or resource for word meanings, spellings and usage.

items.example: Can I borrow a calculator from you for five minutes?
items.note: Borrow means receive something temporarily and return it afterwards; contrast with lend.

items.example: Could you lend me a ruler for the lesson?
items.note: Lend means give something temporarily and expect it back; also lend something to someone.

items.example: Please plug the projector in before the class starts.
items.note: Separable phrasal verb: plug it in. Connect electrical equipment to a socket.

items.example: Could you turn up the volume? The recording is very quiet.
items.note: Make the sound louder; separable: turn it up.

items.example: Turn down the volume while the other group is working.
items.note: Make the sound quieter; separable: turn it down.

items.example: The tutor helped me correct a mistake in my answer.
items.note: Make something right after finding an error.

items.example: It's normal to make a mistake when learning something new.
items.note: Use make, not do, with mistake.

items.pt: trabalhar em dupla; fazer atividade com um colega
items.example: You'll work with a partner on the next exercise.
items.note: Work together with one other person.

items.example: My partner checked my answers after the exercise.
items.note: In class, a partner is another learner you work with.

items.pt: trocar de lugar; trocar de assento
items.example: Shall we swap places so you can see the screen?
items.note: Change where two people sit or stand.

items.pt: dividir um livro com alguém; usar um livro juntos
items.example: We had to share a book because there were not enough copies.
items.note: Use the same book with another person at the same time.

items.example: Repeat after me to practise the final sound.
items.note: A teacher's instruction asking learners to say the same words.

items.example: Would you repeat the last part of the explanation?
items.note: Say or do something again.

items.example: If the meaning is unclear, ask what the word means.
items.note: Question pattern: What does + word or phrase + mean?

items.word: How do you pronounce this word?
items.example: Ask how to pronounce the name before introducing your guest.
items.note: Use How do you pronounce + word or phrase? for pronunciation.

items.word: How do you spell this word?
items.example: If you hear an unfamiliar name, ask how to spell it.
items.note: Use How do you spell + word or phrase? when you want its letters.

items.word: How do you use this word?
items.example: Ask how to use the verb in a polite request.
items.note: A question about normal grammatical or contextual usage.

items.word: explain the difference between two words
items.pt: explicar a diferença entre duas palavras
items.example: Our teacher explained the difference between say and tell.
items.note: Follow difference with between when comparing two words or things.

items.example: What does this expression mean in the article?
items.note: Verb; the corresponding noun is meaning.

items.example: This technical term has a different meaning in physics.
items.note: Noun formed from mean.

items.example: I can pronounce the word, but I cannot spell it yet.
items.note: Verb; the related noun is pronunciation, not pronounciation.

items.example: The pronunciation of this place name surprised me.
items.note: Noun related to pronounce; note the different vowel and spelling.

items.example: Could you spell your surname for the registration form?
items.note: Verb; the related noun is spelling.

items.example: Check the spelling of every heading before printing.
items.note: The written form of a word, or the activity of spelling it.

items.example: Please explain why this answer is correct.
items.note: Verb; explain something to someone is a common pattern.

items.example: Her explanation helped the class understand the rule.
items.note: Noun related to explain.

items.example: A little repetition makes the new pattern easier to remember.
items.note: Noun related to repeat.

items.example: The use of formal language depends on the situation.
items.note: Noun pronounced /juːs/, with an /s/ sound.

items.example: We use this phrase when we apologise.
items.note: Verb pronounced /juːz/, with a /z/ sound.

items.example: Underline the key term with a ruler.
items.note: Useful action mentioned in the ruler exercise as a possible use.

sectionsChecked: A: Equipment and uses; labelled classroom equipment and use examples
B: Classroom activities; instructions, borrowing versus lending language help and student requests

units.title: Unit 32 — School education
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 32. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: British school system, timetable and rules
learningObjectives: Distinguish state and private education and name major stages in the school system of England and Wales.
Use school and exam terminology such as pupil, GCSE, A level, college and vocational training.
Describe lessons, school subjects, timetables, terms and school holidays.
Use natural collocations such as take/do exams, study a subject, break up and go back.
Describe school rules, uniforms, punishment and differences between strict and relaxed schools.

items.example: My cousin attends a state school near her home.
items.note: In the UK, a school funded by the government rather than by fees from parents.

items.example: Her parents pay fees for a private school.
items.note: Here, a fee-paying school, contrasted with a state school.

items.example: State education is free at the point of use in this system.
items.note: Education provided or funded by the government.

items.example: Their youngest child goes to nursery school twice a week.
items.note: Early education for young children before primary school.

items.example: Children usually attend school during the week.
items.note: Attend is a more formal alternative to go to.

items.example: He started primary school at the age of five.
items.note: The first main stage of compulsory school education in this UK outline.

items.pt: escola secundária; ensino fundamental final e médio, conforme o sistema
items.example: Students move to secondary school when they are older.
items.note: School after primary school; stages differ by country.

items.example: Every pupil has a different learning style.
items.note: British English for a student at a school.

items.example: The school system is organised differently across countries.
items.note: How schools and stages of education are arranged.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; prestar um exame
items.example: I'll take an exam at the end of the course.
items.note: Common collocation; do an exam is also possible in this context.

items.example: We have to do an exam in science next month.
items.note: The source accepts both take and do an exam; take is widely used.

items.pt: exames GCSE do ensino secundário britânico
items.example: Pupils in England usually sit GCSE exams during secondary education.
items.note: GCSE is a qualification at the end of a stage of secondary schooling in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; educational systems vary.

items.pt: exames A-level de qualificação pré-universitária britânica
items.example: She is preparing for her A-level exams in June.
items.note: UK subject-based qualifications often taken before university.

items.example: Geography was my favourite subject at school.
items.note: An area studied at school, such as maths or science.

items.pt: faculdade; instituição de ensino pós-secundário; colégio, conforme o contexto
items.example: After school, he enrolled at a local college for training.
items.note: In this UK school context, a place offering further or vocational education; not necessarily a university.

items.example: The college offers vocational training in catering.
items.note: Education focused on skills for a particular job.

items.example: I'm taking a short course in business studies.
items.note: A set of classes covering a subject over a period.

items.example: He decided to stay at school for two more years.
items.note: Continue education at the same school instead of leaving.

items.pt: sair da escola; concluir ou interromper os estudos escolares
items.example: Many young people leave school before starting a job.
items.note: Finish or stop attending school; meaning depends on context.

items.example: She hopes to get a job after finishing her course.
items.note: Obtain employment.

items.pt: seguir para a universidade; continuar os estudos na universidade
items.example: After his final exams, he went on to university.
items.note: Continue education at university after a previous stage.

items.pt: educação continuada; ensino pós-secundário não universitário, no Reino Unido
items.example: She returned to college for further education.
items.note: In the UK, post-school education outside the main university higher-education route.

items.pt: horário de aulas; grade de horários
items.example: Our timetable includes two science lessons on Thursday.
items.note: British English for a schedule of lessons and times.

items.example: Our first lesson begins just after eight.
items.note: A period in which a subject is taught.

items.example: We study several subjects throughout the week.
items.note: The source permits do or study subjects.

items.pt: cursar uma disciplina; estudar uma matéria
items.example: She's doing three subjects this term.
items.note: Informal British usage for studying a school subject.

items.example: I always enjoyed maths at secondary school.
items.note: British English name of the subject; US English usually says math.

items.example: The American textbook calls the subject math.
items.note: American English variant of British maths, explicitly noted in the source.

items.example: We studied local history last term.
items.note: An example of a school subject given in the unit.

items.example: She has science on Monday and Friday.
items.note: An example of a school subject given in the unit.

items.example: We usually go outside during the lunch break.
items.note: A rest period during the school or working day for lunch.

items.example: There's a short break after the second lesson.
items.note: A period of rest between school activities.

items.example: The school year ends in July at her school.
items.note: The annual cycle of school lessons and holidays.

items.pt: período letivo; trimestre ou semestre escolar
items.example: Our school has three terms each year.
items.note: A period of study within the school year; its length varies.

items.example: The day is divided into six lessons.
items.note: Use divided into to describe the parts of a whole, not divided out of.

items.pt: encerrar as aulas; entrar de férias escolares
items.example: Our classes break up for the summer on Friday.
items.note: British English school usage: lessons end for a holiday or term; not the relationship meaning.

items.pt: voltar às aulas; retornar à escola
items.example: The children go back to school in September.
items.note: Return after a holiday or absence.

items.example: Our school rules are displayed near the entrance.
items.note: Instructions about what pupils must and must not do.

items.example: You can get into trouble if you break the rules.
items.note: Do something that is not permitted.

items.example: The teacher did not punish the whole class for one mistake.
items.note: Give a penalty to someone for breaking rules or doing wrong.

items.pt: ficar depois que os outros forem embora
items.example: Two pupils had to stay behind after the lesson.
items.note: Remain in a place after other people have left.

items.pt: escrever uma redação; produzir um ensaio
items.example: I had to write an essay about our town.
items.note: Produce a piece of writing on a particular topic.

items.example: He got into trouble for talking during the test.
items.note: Get into a situation where you may be criticised or punished.

items.example: All pupils at this school wear the same uniform.
items.note: Special clothes required by a school or organisation.

items.example: Students have to wear a uniform on weekdays.
items.note: Use wear for clothes already on your body; put on describes the act of dressing.

items.example: She was not allowed to wear lipstick in class.
items.note: Coloured cosmetic applied to the lips; pictured in the unit.

items.example: The pupil replied, 'Yes, sir.'
items.note: In the passage, a form used by pupils to address a male teacher.

items.example: The pupil asked, 'Excuse me, miss, may I leave?'
items.note: In the passage, a form used by pupils to address a female teacher; practices vary.

items.example: The atmosphere in the classroom was friendly.
items.note: The mood or general feeling in a place.

items.example: The teacher kept the discussion relaxed and informal.
items.note: Comfortable and informal rather than tense or strict.

items.example: Our head teacher was strict about arriving on time.
items.note: A strict teacher expects rules to be followed and may punish rule-breaking.

items.pt: vestir-se; usar determinado tipo de roupa
items.example: At this school, older pupils can dress how they like.
items.note: Here, dress means wear clothes, rather than put on a single garment.

items.example: You need to look smart for the school presentation.
items.note: Here, smart describes neat, suitable clothes, not intelligence.

items.example: Jeans and a plain T-shirt are fine for a casual event.
items.note: Of clothing: informal, not especially smart or formal.
